figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: AFD’s speedup over wide EP balances two gains against one cost (Eq. 1). (1) Batch gain: moving expert weights off attention GPUs frees HBM for larger KV caches and decode batches. (2) Overlap gain: two-microbatch ping-pong hides each microbatch’s MoE behind the other’s attention stage. (3) Disaggregation cost: attention nodes hold KV caches and serve requests; the FFN node does not, so one node in every attention:FFN group produces no tokens.
figures.headline: Batch gain, overlap gain and disaggregation cost are the three factors that set AFD's speedup over wide EP.
citing_sentences: Beyond prediction, we turn the analytical model into a concise key insight: AFD’s speedup over wide EP is the product of two gains and one cost (Figure 1):

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: FastAFD architecture and intra-step ping-pong overlap on GB200 NVL72. (a) Attention nodes (blue) hold paged KV caches and run the attention stage (norms, QKV/O projections, TensorRT-LLM FMHA attention, and top-$K$ routing), while one NVLink round trip per layer (N2M/M2N) dispatches routed tokens to a dedicated FFN node (coral) running a single persistent fused MegaMoE kernel. (b) Splitting each attention GPU’s batch into two ping-pong microbatches (mb0, mb1) overlaps the attention stage on the attention pool with the FFN stage (MegaMoE) on the FFN pool across consecutive layers.
figures.headline: Attention GPUs hold paged KV caches and send routed tokens to one FFN node; splitting batches into two microbatches overlaps the two stages.
citing_sentences: Rather than colocating both modules, AFD Zhu et al. (2025); StepFun et al. (2025) separates MoE inference into an attention pool and a dedicated FFN pool provisioned at a chosen A:F node ratio (Figure 2a).

To overlap them, AFD splits each attention GPU’s batch into two ping-pong microbatches (mb0 and mb1 in Figure 2b): in each layer, while the FFN pool runs mb0’s FFN stage, the attention pool concurrently runs mb1’s attention stage (norms, projections, core attention, and routing), and the two microbatches then swap roles.
Five design choices follow (Figure 2a).

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Context-tuned wide EP narrows homogeneous AFD gains from $1.30\text{--}2.36\times$ to $0.99\text{--}1.17\times$ across 4K–16K contexts. (a) FastAFD speedups over EP4 ($S_{\mathrm{EP4}}$, slate) and over best vLLM wide EP counting all GPUs ($S_{\mathrm{all}}$, coral) or attention GPUs only ($S_{\mathrm{att}}$, teal; stems show the disaggregation cost). (b) Per-GPU batch ratios ($b_{A}/b_{\mathrm{EP4}}$ vs. $b_{A}/b_{V}$). (c) Colocated vLLM scaling across EP4–EP64 normalized to EP4 (outlined markers: per-curve optima).
figures.headline: Context-tuned wide EP shrinks FastAFD's gains over EP4 from 1.30–2.36× to 0.99–1.17× all-GPU speedup.
citing_sentences: In standard decoding across 4K–16K contexts, FastAFD achieves $1.30\text{--}2.36\times$ higher all-GPU throughput than single-node EP4 (Figure 3a, Table 1).

However, scaling colocated vLLM across the rack boosts baseline throughput by $22\text{--}114\%$, peaking at interior widths EP16–EP32 rather than EP64 on every workload (Figure 3c) and compressing FastAFD’s per-GPU batch advantage to $1.06\text{--}1.16\times$ on the full-attention models (Figure 3b).
Against the best wide-EP configuration at each context, FastAFD’s all-GPU speedup $S_{\mathrm{all}}$ narrows to $0.99\text{--}1.17\times$ (Figure 3a; Appendix A).

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Speculative decoding ($d=3,q=4,\bar{a}\approx 1.8$) raises $S_{\mathrm{att}}$ on every workload and keeps $S_{\mathrm{all}}$ at $1.02\text{--}1.13\times$ while contracting optimal A:F ratios (4K–16K). (a) Same-engine speculative self-speedup over $d=0$ (FastAFD up to $1.54\times$). (b) FastAFD speedup over tuned wide EP ($d=0$ circles vs. $d=3$ diamonds): hiding $4\times$ MoE work on the FFN pool raises $S_{\mathrm{att}}$ on all six workloads (up to $1.70\times$) and lifts MiniMax-M2.5 $S_{\mathrm{all}}$ to $1.08\times$ at 4K and 16K. (c) Optimal A:F ratios contract ($d\text{: }0\rightarrow 3$) as the FFN pool takes $rnq$ routed tokens.
figures.headline: Speculative decoding keeps all-GPU speedup at 1.02–1.13× while raising attention-GPU speedup on every workload, up to 1.70×.
citing_sentences: Under speculative decoding at $d=3$ with acceptance controlled near $\bar{a}\approx 1.8$ tokens per step, multi-token verification accelerates both engines across 4K–16K contexts (Figure 4a; Appendix D).

At the same time, verifying four tokens per step contracts FastAFD’s optimal A:F node ratio by more than half on every workload, from 9:1–17:1 down to 4:1–8:1 on MiniMax-M2.5 and from 5:1–11:1 down to 2:1–5:1 on Qwen3 (Figure 4c, Table 2).

Despite dedicating a larger GPU share to FFN nodes, FastAFD lifts $S_{\mathrm{all}}$ on MiniMax-M2.5 from standard-decoding parity up to $1.08\times$ while holding Qwen3 at $1.10\text{--}1.13\times$, and raises $S_{\mathrm{att}}$ across all workloads to $1.22\text{--}1.70\times$ (Figure 4b).

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Three-factor throughput decomposition, step breakdown, and coverage boundary. (a) Equation 1 factors across 4K–16K standard decoding: batch gain $b_{A}/b_{V}$, overlap gain $T_{V}/T_{A}$, disaggregation cost $r/(r{+}1)$, attention-GPU speedup $S_{\mathrm{att}}$, and all-GPU speedup $S_{\mathrm{all}}$. (b) Normalized 8K step share: FastAFD hides colocated MoE while running attention-stage projections twice per step. (c) Ratio of remote FFN latency to the attention stage at 8K, crossing $100\%$ at each model’s measured peak (15:1, 7:1, and 5:1).
figures.headline: FFN latency crosses 100% of the attention stage at each model's measured peak, at 15:1, 7:1 and 5:1.
citing_sentences: Figure 5a shows how each term plays out on the three models.

In the attention stage, $T_{a,\ell}$ combines core attention KV-cache reads with layer norms, QKV/O projections, and top-$K$ routing on the attention GPU, which run once per microbatch and therefore twice per step even when the FFN stage is hidden (Figure 5b).

Below this coverage boundary, remote MoE adds no exposed latency to the critical path, so adding attention nodes per FFN node reduces the disaggregation cost without stretching the step; once the FFN stage exceeds the attention stage (crossing $100\%$ in Figure 5c), uncovered FFN execution lengthens the step directly.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Zero-refit model validation across candidate A:F ratios. (a) At 16K standard decoding ($d=0$), predicted throughput (dashed) against measured throughput (solid) across candidate ratios. (b) At 16K speculative decoding ($d=3$), the model captures the leftward shift of the optimal ratio. (c) Relative error $|\widehat{X}/X-1|$ across all 65 deployments up to each workload’s optimal ratio ($2.9\%$ mean error, dashed line).
figures.headline: Predicted throughput tracks measured throughput across candidate ratios, with mean error of 2.9% over 65 deployments.
citing_sentences: Across all 65 deployments up to each workload’s optimal ratio, the model predicts FastAFD throughput with a mean error of $2.9\%$—specifically $3.0\%$ in standard decoding and $2.6\%$ in speculative decoding—and never exceeds $7.4\%$ on any run (Figure 6c).

At 16K (Figures 6a and 6b), the model accurately reproduces both the standard-decoding throughput curves across all three architectures and the leftward shift of the optimal ratio under speculative decoding.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Runtime ablations at 8K and MoE-boundary vs. tuned CAD across 4K–16K. (a) Fused MegaMoE vs. DeepEP+DeepGEMM at 7:1. (b) Microbatch count $k$ on MiniMax-M2.5 at 3:1 and 7:1. (c) One-step-ahead coordinator on vs. off at 7:1. (d) FastAFD vs. peak-tuned CAD on MiniMax-M2.5 across 4K–16K.
figures.headline: Fused MegaMoE lowers step latency relative to DeepEP plus DeepGEMM, and two microbatches give the lowest step latency.
citing_sentences: Figure 7 evaluates the contribution of each runtime mechanism at 8K context (complete wall-clock measurements in Appendix E).

First, replacing modular DeepEP+DeepGEMM with the fused MegaMoE kernel cuts step latency by $50\%$ on Qwen3 and by $44\%$ on MiniMax-M2.5 at a $7\text{:}1$ ratio (Figure 7a), while avoiding over $12\,\text{GiB}$ of extra buffer memory per attention GPU that causes DeepEP+DeepGEMM to run out of memory at full batch on Qwen3.

Second, sweeping the microbatch count from $k=1$ to $k=4$ on MiniMax-M2.5 confirms that $k=2$ achieves the lowest step latency at both $3\text{:}1$ and $7\text{:}1$ (Figure 7b): $k=1$ serializes attention and FFN execution, whereas $k=3$ and $k=4$ repeat the attention GPUs’ dense projections $k$ times per step and shrink per-microbatch GEMM dimensions.

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Rack-scale A:F provisioning and heterogeneous FFN placement across 4K–16K. (a) Optimal homogeneous node ratios $r^{*}=N_{A}/N_{F}$ in standard decoding ($d=0$): full-attention MoEs fan out from $9{:}1\rightarrow 17{:}1$ (MiniMax-M2.5) and $5{:}1\rightarrow 11{:}1$ (Qwen3), whereas hybrid Qwen3.5 holds $5{:}1$ across 4K–16K. (b, c) Measured speedup over best wide EP in standard ($d=0$) and speculative ($d=3$) decoding when counting all GPUs ($S_{\mathrm{all}}$, coral) or attention GPUs only ($S_{\mathrm{att}}$, solid teal; up to $1.39\times$ and $1.70\times$), plus the modeled zero-FFN-cost ceiling (hatched; up to $1.76\times$ and $2.48\times$).
figures.headline: Modeled zero-FFN-cost ceilings reach 1.76× under standard decoding and 2.48× under speculative decoding.
citing_sentences: Figure 8a tracks how the optimal Attention-to-FFN node ratio $r^{*}=N_{A}/N_{F}$ evolves across context lengths from 4K to 16K under standard decoding.

Placing the FFN pool on non-GPU accelerators removes this disaggregation cost, so per-attention-GPU throughput ($S_{\mathrm{att}}$, solid teal bars in Figures 8b and 8c) directly becomes the per-GPU system speedup.

Even with today’s NVLink communication and overlap schedules unchanged, eliminating the disaggregation cost lifts end-to-end GPU speedups from $0.99\text{--}1.17\times$ to $1.08\text{--}1.39\times$ under standard decoding (Figure 8b) and from $1.02\text{--}1.13\times$ to $1.22\text{--}1.70\times$ under speculative decoding (Figure 8c).

figures.label: Figure A1
figures.caption: Operator split boundary comparison. (a) FastAFD keeps projections and routing on the attention pool around an off-path N2M/M2N round trip to fused MegaMoE. (b) Core Attention Disaggregation (CAD) moves projections to the FFN pool, placing its round trip on the attention critical path and shrinking the attention stage.
figures.headline: FastAFD keeps projections on attention GPUs, while the alternative split places an extra round trip on the attention critical path.

abstract: Attention–FFN disaggregation (AFD) separates attention from the experts of a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model and has been reported to raise decode throughput over colocated serving. Whether this advantage holds on rack-scale NVLink systems such as GB200 NVL72 remains unclear: prior results were obtained on other hardware, against narrower colocated baselines, or with analytical models, whereas production engines serve large MoE models on these systems with wide expert parallelism (wide EP). We build and carefully tune FastAFD, an AFD inference engine for GB200 NVL72 that overlaps the MoE of one microbatch with the attention of the other, and compare it against the best vLLM wide EP setting (with the EP width tuned per workload). Our experiments show that AFD has a throughput advantage of up to $1.17\times$ over wide EP on Qwen3 and $1.16\times$ on Qwen3.5, and matches it on MiniMax-M2.5. We derive an analytical model that predicts AFD throughput within $3\%$ using only profiles of colocated vLLM, which tells whether switching to AFD would improve throughput before AFD is deployed. Beyond prediction, we turn the model into a concise insight: AFD’s speedup factors into a batch gain (larger batches, since attention GPUs hold no expert weights), an overlap gain (shorter steps, since the MoE runs on the expert GPUs behind attention), and a disaggregation cost (the GPUs given to experts). AFD has the advantage when the two gains outweigh the cost. This view explains which models benefit from AFD, and shows that speculative decoding helps light-expert models most, where the enlarged overlap gain outweighs the larger disaggregation cost and adds a further $8\%$ to AFD’s advantage over wide EP. Looking ahead, serving the experts on accelerators that keep their weights in on-chip SRAM, such as the Groq LPX accelerators that NVIDIA pairs with Vera Rubin NVL72, would remove most of the disaggregation cost, raising the ideal speedup to $2.48\times$ with speculative decoding. FastAFD is open source at https://github.com/hao-ai-lab/FastAFD.

sections.body: The paper asks whether attention–FFN disaggregation (AFD) beats colocated wide expert parallelism on GB200 NVL72. Prior evidence comes from older hardware, narrower baselines, or analytical models. The authors build FastAFD, an AFD engine for GB200 NVL72 that overlaps the MoE of one microbatch with the attention of the other. They benchmark it against vLLM wide EP, with the EP width tuned per workload, on three MoE models. AFD reaches up to 1.17× over wide EP on Qwen3-235B at 16K context. An analytical model built only from colocated vLLM profiles predicts AFD throughput within 3% on average. The model splits the speedup into batch gain, overlap gain and disaggregation cost. The paper projects an ideal 2.48× with heterogeneous placement and speculative decoding, and does not measure it.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Whether AFD beats wide EP on GB200 NVL72 is unsettled, so the paper builds FastAFD and benchmarks it against tuned wide EP.

sections.body: Colocated wide EP shards experts across 8–64 GPUs and keeps attention data-parallel. This frees HBM for larger decode batches, but each GPU still runs attention, routing and expert FFN serially. AFD places attention on one pool and experts on a dedicated FFN pool. It splits each attention batch into two ping-pong microbatches so the two pools run in parallel. On NVL72, the 1.8 TB/s NVLink fabric strengthens the colocated baseline, so the comparison must count the FFN GPUs. FastAFD uses the same TensorRT-LLM attention kernels and block-FP8 experts as vLLM. It also uses a fused MegaMoE kernel on FFN GPUs, GPU-initiated communication, and a one-step-ahead CPU coordinator with whole-step CUDA graph capture.
sections.heading: Background and Motivation
sections.headline: Colocated wide EP already frees much of the memory AFD targets, so the comparison must charge AFD for its FFN nodes.

sections.body: The experiments use one GB200 NVL72 rack of 18 four-GPU nodes. The models are MiniMax-M2.5, Qwen3-235B and Qwen3.5-397B in FP8, at 4K, 8K and 16K contexts. Each engine is reported at its best configuration: the vLLM EP width or the FastAFD attention-to-FFN ratio. All-GPU speedup counts the dedicated FFN GPUs. Under standard decoding, MiniMax-M2.5 sits at 1.00–1.02×, Qwen3 reaches 1.06–1.17×, and Qwen3.5 falls to 0.99× at 16K. Speculative decoding uses draft depth 3 with simulated acceptance near 1.8 tokens per step for both engines, so draft quality is not tested. Speculative decoding lifts MiniMax-M2.5 to 1.08× and keeps Qwen3 at 1.10–1.13×.
sections.heading: End-to-End Performance on NVL72
sections.headline: Against tuned wide EP, FastAFD reaches 0.99–1.17× all-GPU speedup under standard decoding and 1.02–1.13× under speculative decoding.

sections.body: All-GPU speedup is factored into a batch gain, an overlap gain, and a disaggregation cost set by the attention-to-FFN node ratio. Qwen3 has heavy experts in all 94 layers, so its overlap gain is largest. MiniMax-M2.5 has light experts, so its step barely changes. On Qwen3.5, batch grows 1.4–1.6×, but its step is slower than wide EP's. The per-layer model takes the maximum of attention and FFN time in each layer and sums over layers. Its inputs come from hardware specifications and one colocated profile per workload, with no parameters fitted to FastAFD runs. Across 65 deployments up to each workload's optimum, mean error is 2.9% and no run exceeds 7.4%. Deploying the model-selected ratio keeps 95–100% of peak throughput in standard decoding.
sections.heading: Understanding the Performance
sections.headline: Batch gain, overlap gain and disaggregation cost together decide each model's regime, and a per-layer model predicts throughput within 2.9% mean error.

sections.body: FastAFD runs a persistent fused MegaMoE kernel on each FFN GPU. It pulls FP8 activations over NVLink and pushes BF16 outputs back without host synchronization. The ablations run at 8K context. Replacing DeepEP plus DeepGEMM with the fused kernel cuts step latency by 50% on Qwen3 and 44% on MiniMax-M2.5 at 7:1. The modular path runs out of memory at full batch on Qwen3. Sweeping the microbatch count shows k=2 gives the lowest step latency at 3:1 and 7:1. Disabling the one-step-ahead coordinator adds 14 ms of host overhead per step and reduces throughput by 32%. A core attention disaggregation variant reaches only 0.68–0.78× of FastAFD's per-GPU throughput, tested on MiniMax-M2.5.
sections.heading: System Implementation and Ablation
sections.headline: Ablations show fused MegaMoE cuts step latency 50% on Qwen3, two microbatches give the lowest latency, and disabling the coordinator costs 32% throughput.

sections.body: On full-attention models the optimal ratio rises with context: from 9:1 to 17:1 on MiniMax-M2.5 and from 5:1 to 11:1 on Qwen3. Qwen3.5 holds 5:1 from 4K to 16K. Speculative decoding with draft depth 3 contracts the ratio by more than half, so FFN nodes take 11–33% of the rack instead of 6–17%. Placing the FFN pool on non-GPU accelerators removes the disaggregation cost. With today's schedules, end-to-end speedups rise from 0.99–1.17× to 1.08–1.39× under standard decoding, and from 1.02–1.13× to 1.22–1.70× under speculative decoding. A zero-FFN-cost bound, where expert weights sit in on-chip SRAM, reaches 1.20–1.76× under standard decoding and 1.38–2.48× under speculative decoding. These bounds are modeled, not measured.
sections.heading: Provisioning and Outlook
sections.headline: Speculative decoding contracts the optimal ratio, and SRAM expert accelerators would raise the modeled ceiling to 2.48× under speculation.

sections.body: The section groups related work by granularity. Request-phase disaggregation and chunked-prefill schedulers separate prefill from decode, and FastAFD runs inside a decode pool. Attention offloading and core attention disaggregation split narrower parts of each layer. MoE-boundary AFD systems split at the routed expert interface, as FastAFD does. Heterogeneous MoE systems such as Fiddler and MoE-Lightning keep expert weights in CPU memory. Vera Rubin NVL72 paired with Groq LPX runs FFN on separate accelerators. Prior speculative decoding studies analyze colocated execution only. Prior rack-scale AFD studies use analytical rooflines or offline simulators. The authors claim the first end-to-end hardware audit on GB200 NVL72 against context-tuned wide EP.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior AFD studies are analytical or on older hardware, and this paper adds an end-to-end GB200 NVL72 audit.

sections.body: The conclusion is that AFD ranges from parity to 1.17× over per-workload-tuned wide EP when every FFN GPU is counted. The authors describe this as a provisioning decision rather than an architectural win. The batch gain, overlap gain and disaggregation cost explain the outcome. A per-layer model calibrated from colocated profiles alone predicts throughput within 3%. An operator can therefore decide before deploying AFD. Speculative decoding and off-GPU expert accelerators are named as the two levers that tilt the balance toward AFD. The evidence covers three MoE models on one GB200 NVL72 rack.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: AFD ranges from parity to 1.17× over tuned wide EP, so the choice depends on provisioning rather than architecture.

sections.body: Table A1 gives the model specifications. Qwen3-235B has 94 layers and 128 experts, MiniMax-M2.5 has 62 layers and 256 experts, and Qwen3.5-397B has 60 layers and 512 experts. Tables A3 to A5 list every measured standard-decode configuration. Table A17 lists the 15 cells of the core attention disaggregation comparison on MiniMax-M2.5. Table A6 summarizes model accuracy over 88 runs, and Table A18 lists the run presets. Measurement rules define FastAFD cells as 1024 output tokens with a mean step over a steady window. vLLM cells use streaming probe requests to time each step. The authors state they recomputed reported results from raw hardware logs.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists model specifications, complete standard-decode tables, residual errors, measurement rules, disaggregation comparison cells, and run presets.
